speaker: Matei Zaharia
title: The Agent Cloud: Databricks' Bet on the Future of AI — Matei Zaharia and Reynold Xin
question: In modern software and AI agent infrastructure, why do formal protocols and APIs still need to be deliberately designed when AI can generate custom integration code on demand?
guest: You have a company maintaining some kind of table, like a Walmart with inventory and what has been sold in each store. And you have suppliers who would love to produce more things and ship them exactly the moment you need them, so they would love real-time access to your table. Instead of sending emails around or Excel sheets or phone calls, why can't you share a view of that table in real time with them? Then they query it, join it with their data, and decide what to send. You might ask today, since we can vibe code anything so fast, why do we even need to design protocols or APIs or software? Can't you just vibe code things on demand? Actually, for this type of interoperability where multiple parties moving at different speeds are building stuff and you still want some layer on top to coordinate, you do want to design it and build it. It reminds me of agents talking to each other and users talking to agents and tools.

points.core: Interoperability across independent parties moving at different speeds requires a shared coordination layer.
points.note: Accept: separately evolving organizations, teams, or systems need an explicit shared contract to stay compatible over time. Do not credit: generic claims that APIs are good software engineering practice or easier to maintain.

points.core: Shared protocols replace brittle ad-hoc handoffs like emailed spreadsheets with live queryable interfaces.
points.note: Accept: real-time shared table views or standardized live data access replacing static files, emails, or manual syncs. Do not credit: vague mentions of real-time data without contrasting against ad-hoc exchange.

points.core: Standardized protocols enable autonomous agents to reliably coordinate across external tools.
points.note: Accept: agents communicating with other agents, users, or external tools via a common protocol layer. Do not credit: generic mentions of MCP or tool calling without explaining multi-party coordination.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because generating code solves the cheap part of integration, not the hard part. A protocol is a shared agreement between independent parties, and no amount of code generation on one side can create agreement on the other.

Deliberately designed interfaces provide things bespoke glue code cannot. They give a stable contract, so both sides can evolve independently without breaking each other; generated code against an undocumented or shifting surface fails silently when that surface changes. They define security and trust boundaries, such as authentication, permission scoping and auditability, which must be enforced by the system itself rather than by whatever a model happened to write. They also specify semantics: error handling, idempotency, versioning and what an operation actually guarantees.

There is also an economic argument. With a standard, such as the Model Context Protocol for agent tools, each tool and each client implements once, instead of every pairing needing its own custom integration that must be generated, tested and maintained. One-off generated code is also unreviewed, non-deterministic and hard to verify at scale.

AI makes writing to an interface nearly free, which raises rather than lowers the value of having a good interface to write to.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Generating integration code on demand reduces only initial authoring cost, not the runtime, security, and maintenance realities of distributed systems. Without shared standards like REST or the Model Context Protocol, connecting many agents and services produces a combinatorial web of bespoke adapters that break whenever upstream systems evolve, turning cheap code generation into a costly maintenance and debugging burden. More fundamentally, APIs and protocols are not mere syntax glue; they are explicit contracts that define domain semantics, state invariants, idempotency, and failure modes. Improvising integrations on the fly introduces probabilistic bugs, schema misinterpretations, and inference latency where fast, deterministic execution is required. Deliberately designed interfaces also enforce non-negotiable trust boundaries—governing authentication, least-privilege permissions, rate limits, and audit trails—while hiding internal implementation details so systems can evolve independently. Far from making formal protocols obsolete, AI agents depend on stable, machine-readable contracts for reliable capability discovery, observability, and safe autonomous execution at scale.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Generated glue code doesn't remove the need for agreements. It just moves the cost to somewhere less visible. A protocol is a shared contract, not just a piece of code. It fixes what the two sides promise each other: what the data means, how errors and retries behave, how versions change, and who is allowed to do what. If an AI writes a custom adapter every time, each one rests on its own guesses about those promises. You get N×M brittle point-to-point integrations that break quietly when either side changes, and nobody can easily test or audit them.

Standards like MCP, OAuth or OpenAPI make behavior predictable and testable. They let tools, security reviews, monitoring and governance work across everything built on them. They also give one place to enforce authentication, permissions and rate limits. That matters even more when the callers are autonomous agents, where an assumption the model invented can turn into a security hole. There are practical reasons too: designed interfaces are cheaper and more reliable than generating code each time, and they allow caching and reuse. Finally, AI writes integrations much better against a clear, well-documented specification. Good protocols make AI-generated code more useful, not less.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Even though AI can write custom glue code on demand, generating code does not eliminate the need for shared, reliable contracts between systems. Formal protocols and APIs establish deterministic boundaries—defining exact data schemas, error semantics, idempotency, and versioning—so integrations behave predictably rather than relying on brittle, probabilistic code that can silently break when an underlying service changes.

Deliberate interface design is also essential for security and governance. Well-structured APIs enforce authentication, least-privilege access, rate limiting, and clear audit trails, ensuring autonomous agents operate within strict guardrails rather than improvising unsafe workarounds.

Finally, protocols solve the scaling problem of interoperability. Without common standards, connecting many agents to many tools devolves into an unmaintainable web of bespoke integrations that incur repeated latency, token overhead, and debugging costs. A thoughtfully designed protocol makes capabilities self-describing, reusable, and independently evolvable, turning ad-hoc code generation into dependable infrastructure.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
AI can generate the code that connects two systems, but those systems still need a shared agreement about what their messages mean, who can perform which actions, and what happens when something fails. A generated integration might retry a payment after a timeout, for example. Only the API’s contract can tell it whether that retry is safe or could charge the customer twice.

A deliberately designed protocol lets independently built systems rely on the same guarantees. Teams can test integrations against it, enforce permissions at the service boundary, and evolve implementations without breaking callers. This matters especially for AI agents, which may discover and invoke tools at runtime. Clear contracts give agents reliable information about what a tool does and give services a way to enforce what an agent is allowed to do. AI makes adapters cheaper to write. The protocol makes their behavior predictable.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
AI can generate code that connects two systems, but someone still has to decide what those systems can promise each other. An agent can write an adapter that retries a payment request after a timeout. Only the payment service can guarantee that a retry won’t charge the customer twice, and its API must tell the agent how to obtain that guarantee.

A deliberately designed protocol makes those decisions explicit and reusable. It defines what operations mean, who may perform them, how failures are reported, and which guarantees survive a version change. Independent teams can then build and test against the same expectations without renegotiating them for every integration. AI lowers the cost of implementing each side of that agreement. The agreement itself is what lets either side trust the result.
